newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD wants special tax on millionaires.
newsitem.headline: German SPD wants special tax on millionaires.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) at the weekend proposed a special levy on the country's 950,000 millionaires as part of a broad tax reform package being discussed with the government.
The proposal would in effect mean the reintroduction of a wealth tax which the ruling coalition abolished this year in the face of bitter opposition from the SPD.
Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the SPD, told Bild am Sonntag newspaper his party wanted millionaires to pay an annual tax of between one and three percent of their wealth.
"It will be a kind of solidarity surcharge for millionaires which will generate 45 to 50 billion marks per year for the state," Scharping was quoted as saying.
The money would go towards funding the welfare system, promoting job creation, financing state aid for east Germany and easing the burden on other taxpayers, Scharping said.
Germans already pay a so-called solidarity income tax surcharge of 7.5 percent to help fund east German development.
Scharping said the tax should be introduced either on January 1, 1998 as part of the overall tax reform package or after the 1998 general election, "when we will have the majority."

The tax was not intended to punish the rich but rather as way for them to show solidarity at a difficult time for the state's finances, Scharping said. An SPD working group would work out details of the proposal by Easter.
The tax could amount to one percent on a wealth of one million marks upwards, two percent from 10 million marks and three percent from 50 million marks, Scharping said.

"The whole thing will have to be introduced with a (backdated) start date so that people don't just suddenly take their money and run. I would like to have January 1, 1997 as the retroactive start date."
The ruling coalition parties and the SPD on Friday agreed to hold a third round of talks on March 8 to try and agree on tax changes aimed at giving jobs and investment in Germany a much-needed boost.
Under discussion is a 30 billion-mark coalition package of tax cuts to be phased in over two years.

It envisages reductions in income and corporate taxes but the SPD opposes a planned cut in the top rate of income tax to 39 percent from 53 and is also against plans to tax income from night shifts and Sunday working.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he still hoped to reach an agreement on tax reforms with the SPD but was prepared to proceed without them.
"We will in any case, that means with or without the SPD, press ahead with our plans for a tax reform," Waigel was quoted telling Bild am Sonntag newspaper in an interview.
Waigel said the government would present a draft for the reform this month.
If no agreement was reached with the SPD the package would have to go before the German parliament's arbitration committee, Waigel said.

"I am still hoping for a settlement in the current talks," Bild am Sonntag quoted Waigel as saying. "That would be better for all involved -- for the SPD as well -- and would be an important signal to kick-start the economy and create jobs."
Failure to agree would condemn the measures to long wrangling in parliament, where the SPD can block tax changes through its majority of the upper house, or Bundesrat.
